Field robot or autonomous tractor? Dutch grower puts both to the test

 02-11 | Field robots | Article

LinkedInFacebookXWhatsAppPrint

Photos: Peter Roek

Which makes more sense on an arable farm: a purpose-built field robot or a conventional tractor equipped with an autonomy retrofit kit? Dutch grower Marijn Vermuë has tested both. After working with an AgXeed AgBot 5.115T2 for an entire season in 2025, he trialled an iQuus-equipped New Holland T6.180 in 2026. His conclusion: both systems are mature enough to justify an investment, although they offer different advantages.

Marijn Vermuë, who farms in Werkendam, North Brabant, spent the 2025 season working with the AgXeed AgBot 5.115T2, a cabless, autonomous tracked tractor. In 2026, he had the opportunity to spend a week working with GPX Solutions’ iQuus system for comparison. This retrofit kit was fitted to a New Holland T6.180. The tractor can work autonomously while remaining a ‘conventional’ tractor that can also be driven by an operator for tasks such as transport.

No competition

A disclaimer: what follows is not the result of a test or competition identifying a winner or the best system. Comparing autonomy systems is not simply a matter of using a tape measure, weighing scales or a points system. It does, however, involve weighing up various factors. Both systems have advantages and disadvantages. How much weight these carry is highly individual, depending on the farm where the system is used and its specific operations. When trying out the New Holland fitted with the iQuus kit in mid-October, Marijn Vermuë focused mainly on operation, ease of use and versatility. Tracks versus wheels and overall weight are relevant considerations, but are not covered in this article.

In 2025, arable farmer Marijn Vermuë experimented with a Kverneland 3400 B plough behind the AgXeed AgBot, among other combinations.‘You cannot go wrong’

Operating the iQuus-equipped tractor is ‘very straightforward’, says Vermuë. ‘The manual takes you through the programme step by step. Foolproof. You cannot go wrong.’ On Tuesday morning, 13 October, it took less than an hour to get the New Holland working for the first time, cultivating a field after potatoes. ‘In the next field, it took less than 10 minutes to get the combination going.’ Vermuë sees little difference in route planning. ‘The iQuus route planning is certainly as practical as AgXeed’s. Both are logical in their own way. They are slightly different, just as Apple’s iOS and Android differ. You need a little time to get used to them.’

Time requirements influence purchasing decisions

Vermuë considers ease of operation and set-up time important. ‘If 10 people end up working with an autonomous tractor over the course of a season, I think it needs to be quick and easy. You could say that an hour here or a few minutes there do not matter, but I consider this a serious point when buying any machine or system for the farm. I do not have unlimited time. Every year seems to fly by. So yes, before every purchase, I look closely at the time involved. That is part of how I run the business. I need to think about it beforehand, because it will not happen later. What I do not want are things that quietly and unintentionally eat up minutes all over the place.’

Vermuë takes the same approach to moving the autonomous tractor to and from the field. The AgBot requires a low-loader, while iQuus requires someone to give him a lift home. In his view, there is little difference in the time involved between the AgBot and an iQuus-equipped tractor. ‘I would rather not stand around for 10 minutes waiting to be picked up. Another option, of course, is to take a bicycle or fatbike along on the tractor.’ Vermuë also wants to point out that iQuus currently cannot work the headlands autonomously. An operator has to drive the tractor for this. He considers it important to include this in the comparison. ‘I understand it will not be long before iQuus can do this too, but AgXeed is not standing still in the meantime either.’

A New Holland tractor equipped with iQuus autonomous control on Marijn Vermuë’s farm in Werkendam. NPPL expert Koen van Boheemen (32) is on the left, with iQuus technician Bas Peijnenburg (25) on the right.Field boundaries are not absolute

One potential advantage for users is that iQuus only requires the implement’s working width to be entered, rather than its length or height as well. ‘That saves time when setting up each operation. On the other hand, the field boundary in iQuus is not absolute, in the sense that implements can swing beyond it. That is often not a problem and can even be efficient alongside a ditch or farm track, but you need to be careful around obstacles. With the AgBot, the field boundary – the geofence – is ‘sacrosanct’.’

You can then decide whether to adjust the route or go ahead anyway, at your own risk, of course

Working right up to the boundaries

Vermuë does see a difference in the approach to safety taken by GPX Solutions and AgXeed. ‘GPX says: this is your boundary, and if you go beyond it, check whether it is safe to do so. AgXeed says: this is your boundary, and the machine can never cross it. How the operator approaches this determines which system is the best fit. Both approaches have advantages and disadvantages. An advantage of iQuus is that the plough can turn over above the ditch. The disadvantage is that, if the route is not planned correctly, the tractor could drive into it. An advantage of AgXeed is that it never allows implements to swing out into the neighbour’s hedge. The disadvantage is that it will never let an implement extend over the ditch. As farmers, we will always look to work right up to those boundaries. We configure the systems to use them as efficiently and safely as possible.’

Transport is one difference: the AgBot needs to be transported, whereas the iQuus-equipped tractor can be driven to the field.Take care!

During set-up and start-up, iQuus issues various warnings if the route is potentially dangerous. For example, if it extends beyond the field or passes too close to obstacles. The warning states very clearly: it may be dangerous to drive this route autonomously. Vermuë says: ‘You can then decide whether to adjust the route or go ahead anyway, at your own risk, of course.’ Joanne de Ruiter of GPX Solutions confirms that the company does not make the geofence completely restrictive. ‘We could, but then customers would say: “We do not want it.”’ In practice, customers make that decision themselves, just as they do when they are driving the tractor.’

One system on 2 tractors: €75,000

To weigh up the 2 systems more fully, Marijn Vermuë also wants to know what it would cost to use an iQuus system on different tractors: for example, a heavier tractor for cultivation and a lighter one for crop care operations. He is therefore interested in what needs to be installed on both tractors and which components can be transferred. ‘What appeals to me about being able to transfer the system from one tractor to another is that, alongside carrying out certain crop care operations autonomously with a relatively small tractor, you could also perform heavy tasks such as deep spading autonomously for a relatively modest additional investment.’

GPX Solutions explains that, if a system costs approximately €50,000, half of that covers components permanently installed on the tractor. The other half covers components that can be transferred to a second tractor that has also been prepared. Preparing each tractor costs €25,000, while the transferable part of the system costs €25,000. That brings the total for 2 tractors to €75,000.

translationZh:
**田间机器人还是自动驾驶拖拉机？荷兰种植者实测两者**

在耕地上，哪种方案更合理：专用田间机器人，还是配备自动驾驶改装套件的传统拖拉机？荷兰种植者Marijn Vermuë对两者都进行了测试。在2025年整个季节使用AgXeed AgBot 5.115T2之后，他于2026年试用了一台搭载iQuus系统的New Holland T6.180。他的结论是：两套系统都已成熟到足以证明投资合理，但它们提供的优势各不相同。

在 Noord-Brabant 省 Werkendam 耕作的 Marijn Vermuë 在2025年季节使用了 AgXeed AgBot 5.115T2——一台无驾驶室的自主履带式拖拉机。2026年，他有机会用一周时间对比测试 GPX Solutions 的 iQuus 系统。该改装套件安装在 New Holland T6.180 上。这台拖拉机可以在自主作业的同时，仍然是一台“常规”拖拉机，也可由驾驶员操作执行运输等任务。

**并非竞争**

先声明：以下内容并非测试或竞赛结果，不判定赢家或最佳系统。比较自动驾驶系统并非简单用卷尺、秤或评分系统就能完成。但它确实涉及权衡各种因素。两套系统各有优缺点。这些因素权重多大高度个性化，取决于使用系统的农场及其具体作业。在10月中旬试用搭载 iQuus 套件的 New Holland 时，Marijn Vermuë 主要关注操作、易用性和多功能性。履带与轮式以及整机重量是相关考量，但本文不涉及。

**“不会出错”**

Vermuë 说，操作搭载 iQuus 的拖拉机“非常直接”。“手册一步步带你走完程序。万无一失。你不会出错。”10月13日周二上午，让这台 New Holland 首次作业——在土豆收获后耕作一块地——用了不到一小时。“在下一块地，让组合开始作业用了不到10分钟。”Vermuë 认为路线规划差别不大。“iQuus 的路线规划肯定和 AgXeed 一样实用。两者各有逻辑。略有不同，就像苹果 iOS 和安卓的区别。需要一点时间适应。”

**时间要求影响购买决策**

Vermuë 认为操作便捷性和设置时间很重要。“如果一个季节下来有10个人使用这台自动驾驶拖拉机，我认为它必须快速简单。你可能会说这里一小时、那里几分钟无所谓，但我认为购买任何机器或系统时这都是严肃的问题。我没有无限的时间。每年似乎都飞逝。所以是的，每次购买前，我都会仔细考虑涉及的时间。这是我经营业务的一部分。我必须事先考虑，因为事后不会发生。我不想要的是那些悄悄无意地到处吞噬分钟的事情。”

Vermuë 对自动驾驶拖拉机往返田间也持同样态度。AgBot 需要低平板车运输，而 iQuus 需要有人接他回家。他认为 AgBot 和搭载 iQuus 的拖拉机在时间上差别不大。“我宁愿不站在那里等10分钟被人接。当然，另一个选择是在拖拉机上带一辆自行车或胖胎车。”Vermuë 还想指出，iQuus 目前无法自主作业地头。操作员必须驾驶拖拉机完成这部分。他认为将其纳入比较很重要。“我知道 iQuus 不久就能做到这一点，但 AgXeed  meanwhile 也没有停滞不前。”

**田块边界并非绝对**

对用户的一个潜在优势是，iQuus 只需输入机具的工作宽度，而不需要输入长度或高度。“这在设置每次作业时节省时间。另一方面，iQuus 中的田块边界不是绝对的，意思是机具可以摆出边界。这通常不是问题，甚至在地沟或农场道路旁可能很高效，但在障碍物周围需要小心。使用 AgBot 时，田块边界——地理围栏——是‘神圣不可侵犯的’。”

**作业到边界**

Vermuë 确实看到 GPX Solutions 和 AgXeed 在安全方法上的差异。“GPX 说：这是你的边界，如果你越过它，检查是否安全。AgXeed 说：这是你的边界，机器永远不能越过。操作员如何处理这一点决定哪个系统最合适。两种方法各有优缺点。iQuus 的一个优势是犁可以在地沟上方翻转。缺点是，如果路线规划不正确，拖拉机可能开进沟里。AgXeed 的一个优势是它永远不允许机具摆入邻居的树篱。缺点是它永远不会让机具伸过地沟。作为农民，我们总是希望作业到这些边界。我们配置系统以尽可能高效和安全地使用它们。”

**小心！**

在设置和启动期间，如果路线有潜在危险，iQuus 会发出各种警告。例如，如果路线超出田块或经过障碍物太近。警告非常明确：自主行驶此路线可能危险。Vermuë 说：“然后你可以决定是调整路线还是继续，当然风险自负。”GPX Solutions 的 Joanne de Ruiter 确认公司不会让地理围栏完全限制性。“我们可以，但客户会说：‘我们不想要那样。’”实践中，客户自己做出决定，就像他们驾驶拖拉机时一样。

**两台拖拉机一套系统：75,000欧元**

为了更全面权衡两套系统，Marijn Vermuë 还想知道在不同拖拉机上使用 iQuus 系统的成本：例如，一台较重的拖拉机用于耕作，一台较轻的用于作物护理作业。因此他关心两台拖拉机上需要安装什么以及哪些组件可以转移。“能够将系统从一台拖拉机转移到另一台，吸引我的是，除了用相对较小的拖拉机自主执行某些作物护理作业外，你还可以以相对适度的额外投资自主执行深松等重活。”

GPX Solutions 解释说，如果一套系统成本约50,000欧元，其中一半覆盖永久安装在拖拉机上的组件。另一半覆盖可转移到第二台也已准备好的拖拉机的组件。准备每台拖拉机花费25,000欧元，而系统的可转移部分花费25,000欧元。两台拖拉机总计75,000欧元。
author: Leo Tholhuijsen
